Imagine that for half an hour you have been driving along a familiar road, absorbed in conversation — and suddenly you realize you cannot remember the last ten kilometers. Your eyes saw the lane markings, your hands turned the wheel, the ache in your stiff back never went anywhere. All of these were mental states — visual, motor, painful. But were they conscious? Intuition suggests: not quite. Something in them switched on only now, when you caught yourself at it. Higher-order theory (HOT) takes this intuition and turns it into a thesis of almost mathematical rigor: a mental state is conscious if and only if there is a higher-order representation to the effect that you are in it.

The key move is the distinction between a state and the awareness of a state. You have pain (a first-order state; it represents damage to the body). And you have — or do not have — the thought "I am now experiencing pain" (a higher-order state; it represents not the world but your own mind). Rosenthal asserts: the pain is not conscious on its own. What makes it conscious is the second, superimposed representation. Unconscious pain is not an oxymoron but a routine occurrence: it guides behavior, makes you shift your posture, but does not "glow" from within until the metacognitive apparatus picks it up. The phenomenal "what-it-is-like-to-be" turns out to be not a property of the experience itself but a property of the experience-about-which-I-am-thinking.

Consciousness is not the basic layer of the psyche but its comparatively late, rare, and fragile upper story. Most of the mind's work goes on in the dark. The light switches on where the mind turns back on itself. Metacognition — the representation of one's own states — is then not an ornament of consciousness but its constitutive condition. Herein lies the theory's charm: it promises to explain consciousness through an intelligible currency — representations and thoughts about representations — without invoking either new fundamental entities or a mysterious "mental radiance."

How it came about. HOT's pedigree is customarily traced back to Locke with his famous formula that consciousness is "the perception of what passes in a man's own mind." The modern version was built by David Rosenthal, beginning with the programmatic paper "Two Concepts of Consciousness" (1986) and continuing through a series of works collected in the book Consciousness and Mind (2005). His variant is called higher-order thought theory: the relevant higher-order representation is a thought, an assertoric judgment about one's state. In parallel, William Lycan in Consciousness and Experience (1996) developed higher-order perception theory: the mind not so much thinks about its states as inwardly perceives them by a special "inner sense" (an idea going back to Kant and Locke). The difference is not cosmetic: perception is less conceptually loaded than thought and answers objections differently. Later came "self-representational" variants, in which a state represents itself without a separate superstructure, and Hakwan Lau with Rosenthal, in a paper in Trends in Cognitive Sciences (2011), tried to ground the theory in neuroscience, linking conscious access to activity of the prefrontal cortex rather than only the sensory areas.

Criticism / arguments against. The sharpest objection is the misrepresentation problem (or the problem of "empty targets," targetless HOTs). The theory's logic is merciless: consciousness is constituted by the higher-order thought. But thoughts, like all representations, can be false. What if the thought "I am experiencing pain" is there, but the state of pain at the lower level is not? By the theory's own logic the subject must then consciously experience a nonexistent pain. In that case the bearer of the phenomenology turns out to be not the experience but the thought about it — and the first-order state becomes superfluous altogether. Critics (Ned Block, Karen Neander, Joseph Levine) conclude: either the theory refutes itself, or it quietly shifts the whole phenomenal burden onto the higher order, turning into a disguised first-order theory. Rosenthal replies that in such cases it seems to the subject that they are in the state — and that "seems" is enough, but to critics such as Block this answer looks like a confession: consciousness is then simply the content of the higher-order thought, and the lower story is decorative.

The second objection is the threat of infinite regress. If a state is conscious only when there is a thought about it, must not this thought itself become conscious — through a third-order thought, and so on, ad infinitum? Rosenthal blocks the regress with a proviso: the higher-order thought is usually not itself conscious (we are not aware of the act of awareness); it makes the lower state conscious while remaining in the shadows. This saves the theory from regress, but with a strange implication: that which bestows the light itself abides in the dark — and opponents ask how an unconscious thought can generate phenomenal brightness at all.

The third front is the dispute with rivals. Global Workspace Theory (GWT, Baars, Dehaene) says: a state is conscious when it is "broadcast" to the whole cognitive system and becomes globally available — no separate thought about the state is required; what matters is access, not meta-representation. First-order theories (Fred Dretske, Michael Tye) go further: phenomenality already lives in the first-order representations of the world themselves, and reflection is merely added on top. Integrated Information Theory (IIT, Tononi) changes the coordinate system entirely: consciousness is a measure of integrated information Φ, a property of the causal structure, indifferent to whether the system thinks about itself. Against this backdrop HOT risks confusing consciousness with the introspective report about consciousness — the ability to report an experience, rather than the ability to experience. The objection from animals and infants strikes the same point: if pain requires a conceptually formed thought "I am in a state of pain," then creatures without developed metacognition formally end up in the dark — a conclusion that Dretske, Tye and William Seager, among others, count against the theory, while Peter Carruthers is prepared to accept it.

What to do about it / where it leads. For alignment, HOT is not a museum exhibit but a working tool, and precisely for that reason a dangerous one. In the report "Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence" (Butlin, Long et al., 2023), the authors address the question "is the AI conscious" by assessing computational features. They extract from the leading theories of consciousness a set of indicator properties — computational features that a theory links to consciousness — and check whether those features are realizable in architectures. HOT, among others, yields a fairly concrete indicator: the presence of a metarepresentation mechanism, that is, a model representing the system's own states and their reliability (the report takes this indicator from Hakwan Lau's perceptual reality monitoring theory, a computational version of HOT). Modern AIs already contain something similar: models calibrate confidence and represent their own uncertainty; conversational agents glibly deliver reports about "their states." The temptation to read this as a marker of nascent consciousness is enormous.

But fluent self-report can be an imitation of introspection. Training a system to generate convincing utterances such as "it hurts," "I am afraid of being shut down," does not establish that it has the perceptual representations and metacognitive monitoring required by these indicators. David Chalmers also warns against this methodological trap in his analysis of the consciousness of large language models: a fluent self-report is the weakest kind of evidence, because it is the very thing that training optimizes.

The practical conclusion is twofold. On one hand, an AI's self-modeling and metacognition are a real and useful object of interest: a system that accurately represents its own states and the boundaries of its knowledge is safer and more intelligible, and by HOT's logic it is also the nearest computational neighbor of consciousness. On the other hand, HOT's computational indicators require more than verbal self-description. Before treating an AI's self-reports as indicators of consciousness, one should ask whether they reflect the perceptual representations and higher-order monitoring described by the theory. Until we can answer this question, it is more honest to keep an AI's metacognitive abilities in the column "morally significant uncertainty" rather than "proof of consciousness."
